Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 68, verses 1–3:

﴿Nun﴾ is one of the letters of the alphabet (huruf al-hijaʾ, the disjointed letters). Its discussion has already passed in al-Baqara. What is specific to ﴿Nun﴾ is that it has been said that it is a letter from al-Rahman (the Most Merciful), since the letters of al-Rahman are alif, lam, ra, ha, mim, and nun. It has also been said that the nun here refers to the fish, and from this comes Dhu al-Nun (the Man of the Fish), Yunus. ﴿By the pen and what they inscribe﴾. This has been disputed, with two opinions. The first is that it is the pen with which the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) was written, so the pronoun in "they inscribe" refers to the angels. The second is that it is the pen known among people, which God swore by because of the benefits and wisdom in it, and the pronoun in "they inscribe" according to this refers to the children of Adam. ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman﴾. This is the answer to the oath, and it is addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ). Its meaning is the negation of what the disbelievers attribute to him of madness. "By the grace of your Lord" is a parenthetical insertion between "not" (ma) and its predicate, just as you say, "You are, by the power of God, the best." The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Al-Zamakhshari said: the element governing it is "a madman." ﴿Unending﴾ is mentioned in Fussilat [8].

﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character.﴾ This is praise for the character (khuluq) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "The character of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the Qur'an." The details of this are that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) combined every virtue and possessed every good quality: nobility of lineage, abundance of intellect, soundness of understanding, great knowledge, intense modesty, frequent worship, generosity, truthfulness, courage, patience, gratitude, manliness, kindness, moderation, asceticism, humility, compassion, justice, forgiveness, restraint of anger, maintaining family ties, good companionship, good management, eloquence of tongue, strength of the senses, beauty of form, and other qualities, as is recorded in his reports and biography (ﷺ). First, that it is extra (zāʾida).
Second, that it is not extra, and the meaning is "which of you is the affliction," so that al-maftūn is placed in the position of al-fitna, as in their saying: mā lahu maʿqūl, meaning ʿaql (he has no reason).
Third, that the bāʾ means fī (in), and the meaning is "in which group among you is the afflicted one." Ibn ʿAṭiyya approved this view.
Fourth, that the meaning is "which of you is the affliction of the afflicted one," then the modified noun (al-muḍāf) was deleted and the modifier (al-muḍāf ilayhi) was put in its place.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 68, verses 9–16:

﴿They wish you would soften (toward them), so they would soften (toward you).﴾ *Al-mudahana* (flattery, a yielding in matters where it is not proper) means softening and tolerance in what should not be tolerated. It is narrated that the disbelievers said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you worshipped our gods, we would worship your God." So the verse was revealed. *Fayudhinun* (so they would soften) is not in the subjunctive as a response to the wish (*jawab al-tamanni*, the answer to an expressed wish). Rather, it is in the nominative by coordination with *tudhin* (you soften). This is what Ibn 'Atiyya said. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its meaning being "so they are softening."

﴿Who swears much﴾: one who swears often, in truth and falsehood.
﴿Contemptible﴾: one who is weak in opinion and intellect. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it derives from *mahun*, meaning weak, so the *mim* is the first radical of the verb. Al-Zamakhshari said: it derives from *mahana* (contemptibility), which is abasement and lowliness. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-mahin* is the liar.

﴿Backbiter﴾: one who disparages people.
﴿Going about as a slanderer﴾: one who walks much carrying tale-bearing. *Namim* and *namima* have the same meaning. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The slanderer will not enter Paradise."

﴿Hindering the good﴾: that is, niggardly, because "the good" here means wealth. It is also said: the meaning is one who hinders people from Islam and righteous deeds.

﴿Transgressor﴾: from *al-'udwan*, which is injustice.
﴿Sinful﴾: from *al-ithm*, which is committing what is forbidden.

﴿Violent﴾ (*'utull*): one of coarse body, hard of heart, far from understanding, and abundant in ignorance.
﴿Base-born﴾ (*zanim*): the illegitimate son. It is also said: one who has a *zanama* (fleshy appendage) on his neck, like the wattle of a sheep hanging from its throat. It is also said: its meaning is one who is suspicious and of evil deeds. It is also said: a wrongdoer; and it is said: a base person.

His saying ﴿after all that﴾ means after what we have mentioned of his defects. This ordering in the description is not one of time.

The scholars differed about who is described by these blameworthy attributes. It is said: none particular is intended, but rather everyone who has these qualities. It is said: the intended person is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, because (God) described him as possessing wealth and sons, and so he was. It is said: Abu Jahl. It is said: al-Akhnas ibn Shariq. This supports the view that he had a wattle on his neck. Ibn 'Abbas said: "We recognized him by his wattle; he was a foundling from Thaqif, and he was counted among the Banu Zuhra." So describing him as *zanim* is correct on both views. It is also said: al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth.

﴿Because he has wealth and sons﴾: this is in the position of a causal object (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), governed by His saying ﴿do not obey﴾. That is, do not obey him because of the abundance of his wealth and sons. It is permissible for it to be governed by what follows it, and the meaning on this reading is that he said of the Qur'an "tales of the ancients" because he possesses wealth and sons and is arrogant with his wealth and sons. The governing element of *an kana* (because he was) on this reading is a verb implied by the meaning. The verb *qala* (he said), which is the answer of *idha* (when), cannot govern it, because what follows a conditional cannot govern what precedes it. The first view is more evident. The meaning of "tales of the ancients" has already been mentioned.

﴿We will brand him upon the snout﴾: the original meaning of *al-khurtum* is the nose of a beast of prey. It was then borrowed for a human, to belittle and disgrace him. The meaning is: We will make for him a mark (*sima*), which is a sign upon his snout. The scholars differed about this mark. It is said: it is the sword strike on the day of Badr. It is said: a mark of fire placed on his nose in Hell. It is also said: a mark placed on his nose on the Day of Resurrection by which he will be recognized.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 68, verse 35–38:

﴿Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle) here is for denunciation (inkar), meaning: how could Allah make the Muslims equal to the criminals? Note on the verse text: the quoted Qur'anic words above are as they appear in the passage; I translate the passage itself below.

This is a challenge to the disbelievers (taʻjiz). Its meaning: "If you have partners who are able to do anything, then bring them forth." It is disputed whether the words "then let them bring them" (fa-l-ya'tu bihim) refer to this world, that is, "produce them so that their condition may be seen," or whether it will be said to them that on the Day of Resurrection. The partners (al-shuraka') are the deities worshipped, such as idols and others. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is, "Or do you have people who share with you in this claim and agree with you about it? Then bring them." That is, none of them agrees with them on it. The first view is more apparent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 68, verse 42:

﴿On the Day when a shin will be laid bare﴾ The interpreters (al-mutawwilun) said: this is an expression for the terror of the Day of Resurrection and its severity. In the authentic hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) he said: "A caller will call out on the Day of Resurrection: Let every community follow what it used to worship. So whoever used to worship the sun will follow the sun, whoever used to worship the moon will follow the moon, and everyone will follow what he used to worship. Then this community will remain, along with some remnants of the People of the Book, and their hypocrites with them. They will be asked: What is your situation? They will say: We are waiting for our Lord. He said: Then Allah will come to them in other than the form in which they knew Him, and He will say: I am your Lord. They will say: We seek refuge in Allah from you. He said: He will say: Do you recognize Him by a sign you see? They will say: Yes. Then a shin will be laid bare for them, and they will say: Yes, You are our Lord. They will fall down in prostration, and every believer will prostrate, but the backs of the hypocrites will turn into one solid bone, so they will be unable to prostrate." The explanation of the hadith is like the explanation of the verse ﴿and they are summoned to prostration﴾, whose interpretation is in the hadith we have mentioned.

If it is said: How are they summoned to prostration in the Hereafter, when the Hereafter is not an abode of obligation (taklif)?

The answer: They are summoned to it as a rebuke to them for their abandoning prostration in this world, not as an obligation or act of worship.

﴿And they had been called to prostration while they were sound.﴾ That is, in the world they used to be called to prostration and refused it, while they were sound in their limbs and able to perform it.

﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse﴾ is a threat to those who deny the Qur'an. As for its i'rab (grammatical analysis, or syntactic parsing), the phrase ﻣَﻦ ﻳُﻜَﺬِّﺏُ ("those who deny") may be parsed as an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ah) or as a conjoined element (ma'tuf). We have discussed this in Surah al-A'raf [182], where it says ﴿We will draw them on gradually﴾ and what follows.

"Or do you ask them for a reward, so that they are burdened with debt?" — no, translating faithfully:

﴿Or do you ask them for a wage?﴾ Its meaning: you do not ask them for a payment for Islam, so that it would be burdensome to them, and so they have no excuse for abandoning Islam. We have explained this and what follows it in Surat al-Tur [40].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 68, verses 48–49:

﴿So be patient﴾ implies conciliation with the disbelievers, which was abrogated by the sword. ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾: he is Yunus (peace be upon him), and he was called "the companion of the fish" because the fish swallowed him. He is also called Dhu'l-Nun, and al-Nun is the fish. We have mentioned his story in (surah) al-Anbiya' and (surah) al-Saffat. God forbade Muhammad (ﷺ) from being like him in impatience and haste, when he went off in anger. It is related that this verse was revealed when the Prophet (ﷺ) resolved to invoke curses upon the disbelievers. ﴿When he called out while he was suppressing (his grief)﴾: this is the last of what happened to Yunus, and his calling out was his saying in the belly of the fish: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I was among the wrongdoers." Al-makzum is one who is intensely grieved. ﴿He would have been cast out onto the open plain while he was blameworthy﴾: this is the answer to "lawla" (had it not been). What is negated is the blame, not his being cast out onto the open plain, for He said in al-Saffat: ﴿So We cast him onto the open plain﴾ [al-Saffat: 145]. So the meaning is: had it not been for the mercy of God, he would have been cast out onto the open plain while blameworthy, but he was cast out while not blameworthy. We have mentioned al-'Ara' (the open plain) in al-Saffat.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 68, verse 51:

﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost slip you off with their eyes﴾ is an expression for the intensity of their enmity. The "in" (إن) here is the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy "inna" (إن المثقلة), as shown by the entry of the lam (اللام) after it. ﴿Layuzliqunaka﴾ means they would destroy you, like your saying: "So-and-so looked at his enemy with a look that would have thrown him down." Its origin is from the slipping of the foot (زلق القدم). Nafi' recited it with a fatha on the ya' (يُزْلِقونك with ya' opened, read as لَيَزْلِقُونَكَ), and the rest recited it with a damma, and both are dialects (لغتان). It was also said: the meaning is that they strike him with the evil eye (يأخذونه بالعين). This happened among the Banu Asad: a man among them would go hungry for three days, then he would not speak of anything without striking it with the evil eye. Some of them wanted to strike the Prophet (ﷺ) with it, but Allah protected him from that. Al-Hasan said: the cure for one who has been struck by the evil eye is the recitation of this verse.
﴿And it is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾. He means the Qur'an, or it is an admonition and a reminder for creation.
